exercises.objective: Compute and compare the parameter count of a convolutional layer vs. a fully-connected layer on the same input.
exercises.prompt: For a $32\times32\times3$ (RGB) input, compute the number of parameters in a convolutional layer with $C'=16$ output channels and kernel size $k=3$ (using $C'Ck^2$). Enter an integer.
hints: $432$ parameters, compared to a fully-connected layer mapping the same input to 16 outputs, which would need $32\times32\times3\times16=49{,}152$ parameters, about 114 times more, and that ratio only gets worse for larger images, since the FC count scales with image size while the conv count doesn't.

exercises.objective: Match CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures to the structural assumption each is built around.
exercises.prompt: For each scenario, state which architecture family (CNN, LSTM/GRU, or Transformer) is the natural fit, and why: (a) classifying objects in a photograph, (b) predicting the next value in a long, evolving sensor time series, (c) processing a variable-length, unordered set of detected objects where you don't know in advance how they relate to each other.
hints: (a) CNN: photographs have spatial/grid structure, nearby pixels are related, and convolution's weight sharing exploits exactly that (translation invariance).
(b) LSTM/GRU: a sensor time series has sequential/temporal structure, and gated memory (forget/input/output gates) is built specifically to carry information forward across time steps.

(c) Transformer: with no known a-priori order or grid structure, a Transformer's permutation-invariant attention lets every element attend to every other element and *learn* whatever relational structure exists from the data itself, rather than assuming it architecturally.

exercises.objective: Explain why 1/sqrt(h) weight initialization scaling prevents activation scale from drifting across network depth.
exercises.prompt: Explain why initializing each weight in $W_{l,i\cdot}$ with standard deviation $1/\sqrt{h_{l-1}}$ (rather than, say, standard deviation 1 regardless of layer width) helps keep activation scale roughly constant from layer to layer.
hints: A pre-activation $z_i=\sum_{j=1}^{h_{l-1}}W_{ij}x_j$ sums $h_{l-1}$ roughly-independent terms; for independent random terms, the variance of a sum grows linearly with the number of terms summed.

So if each $W_{ij}$ has variance $v$, and each $x_j$ has variance $\text{Var}\{x\}$, then $\text{Var}\{z_i\}\approx h_{l-1}\cdot v\cdot\text{Var}\{x\}$: without correcting for $h_{l-1}$, wider layers would produce systematically larger pre-activations purely from summing more terms, nothing to do with the actual learned structure.

Choosing $v=1/h_{l-1}$ (standard deviation $1/\sqrt{h_{l-1}}$) exactly cancels the $h_{l-1}$ factor, giving $\text{Var}\{z_i\}\approx\text{Var}\{x\}$ regardless of layer width: activation scale is preserved layer to layer instead of compounding (shrinking or exploding) with depth, exactly the ODE-02/DYN-06-style stability concern this module connects to.

exercises.objective: Explain dropout's interpretation as approximating an ensemble of exponentially many networks.
exercises.prompt: Explain why dropout can be understood as training and approximately averaging an ensemble of exponentially many different networks, and why scaling activations by $p$ at prediction time approximates that average.
hints: Each specific pattern of which units happen to drop out on a given training step defines a distinct, smaller sub-network (with some units simply absent); since there are exponentially many possible drop-out patterns, training with dropout is like training an enormous ensemble of different sub-networks, all sharing the same underlying weights.
At prediction time, you'd ideally want to average the predictions of every one of these exponentially many sub-networks, which is computationally infeasible to do explicitly.

Scaling each activation by $p$ (the keep-probability) at prediction time approximates this average directly: on average across training, each unit was 'present' a fraction $p$ of the time, so scaling by $p$ approximates what the ensemble-averaged activation would have been, without ever having to enumerate or run the exponentially many sub-networks explicitly.
